survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses secondary microdata from the first PIAAC cycle (2011–2012, 2014–2015, 2017–2018) and extracts a working-age subsample (adults aged 16–65 who were employed at the time of data collection). The manuscript does not report the use of PIAAC sampling weights or any replicate-weight procedure; therefore, it is unclear whether estimates were adjusted to be population-representative within each country. Because the analysis is based on factor analysis (EFA/CFA) and hierarchical multiple regression rather than PV-based achievement scaling, the paper does not describe PV-specific weighting steps. Analysts using PIAAC microdata should apply the official PIAAC student/household sampling weights (and replicate weights if variance estimation is required) when producing population-representative inferences; however, this paper’s weighting strategy is not documented.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The dependent variable is Informal Learning Behaviors (ILBs) measured via Likert-scale questionnaire items aggregated into a factor score/scale, not a cognitive achievement score with PIAAC Plausible Values. Because the study does not report any PV generation/combining procedure and instead uses psychometric modeling and regression on the extracted item-based constructs, PV handling is not applicable. The manuscript also does not document how missing responses were handled for the analytic sample, so missing-data handling cannot be classified from the provided text.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used PIAAC first cycle microdata and extracted a subsample of 122,897 adults aged 16–65 who were working when data collection took place. Participants were required to answer all items of the study variables (Autonomy in the Workplace, Interaction in the Workplace, Readiness to Learn, and ILBs items). The authors randomly split the extracted sample into three databases (n=61,560; n=30,606; n=30,731) for EFA and CFA model testing, and used the full extracted sample for the hierarchical multiple regression predicting ILBs. No country-level inclusion/exclusion criteria are described beyond the fact that PIAAC first-cycle data were collected across 21 countries in round 1, 8 in round 2, and 5 in round 3.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Hierarchical multiple regression: Model 1 R²=0.093 (F=984.838, p<0.001); Model 2 R²=0.212 (F=3846.559, p<0.001). Interaction in the workplace: b=0.29, SE=0.00, p<0.001, 95% CI for B [0.28, 0.30]. Readiness to learn: b=0.26, SE=0.00, p<0.001, 95% CI for B [0.25, 0.27]. Workplace autonomy: b=0.02, SE=0.00, p<0.001, 95% CI for B [0.01, 0.03].
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PIAAC first-cycle data (2011–2012, 2014–2015, 2017–2018) for a working adult subsample aged 16–65, the study leveraged Interaction in the workplace, Readiness to learn, and Workplace autonomy (plus demographic and work controls) to predict Informal learning behaviors (ILBs), finding that Interaction in the workplace and Readiness to learn were positive predictors while Workplace autonomy had a small positive effect in the regression (and the abstract reports autonomy as resulting in lower ILB scores). This indicates that workplace designs that foster interpersonal interaction and support workers’ readiness to learn may strengthen informal learning behaviors, though the study is cross-sectional and does not establish causal effects.

data.outcome_summary: The study uses PIAAC first-cycle microdata (2011–2012, 2014–2015, 2017–2018) and extracts a working subsample of 122,897 adults aged 16–65 who answered all ILB-related items. It first re-estimates the measurement structure of ILBs and antecedents using EFA and CFA, selecting an 18-item, four-factor model (after excluding two items) with reported fit indices (e.g., CFA for the 18-item model: CFI=0.94, TLI=0.93, RMSEA=0.05, SRMR=0.04). For prediction, it applies hierarchical multiple regression: R² increases from 0.093 (controls only) to 0.212 after adding the three antecedent factors, with Interaction in the workplace showing the largest standardized effect (b≈0.29, p<0.001) and Readiness to learn also significant (b≈0.26, p<0.001). The paper does not report survey-weight usage or missing-data handling, and the analysis is not a machine-learning predictive pipeline; therefore, results should be interpreted as associations rather than causal impacts.
